713735.t: From the same root as χαίρω (khaírō, “to be happy”).

713754.t: Two theories: * According to Strong's Biblical Concordance, from χαράσσω (khărắssō, “to scratch; to inscribe”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰer- (“to scratch”) (compare Lithuanian žerti (“to scrape”)).

713718.t: Likely related to χαῦνος (khaûnos, “porous, loose-grained”) (via an earlier form χάος (kháos) < *χάϝος (*kháwos)), with original meaning "hole, empty space, yawning opening"; from this spring the traditional connections with χάσκω (kháskō, “to gape,…

713781.t: Unknown. The traditional derivation from a Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout”), and subsequent comparison with Old Norse gjǫlnar (“mustache, bearded lips”) and Old Armenian ձեղուն (jełun, “ceiling, palate”), is unconvincing.

713727.t: From χαράσσω (kharássō, “to scratch, engrave”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, agent noun suffix). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀏𐀨𐀏𐀳𐀨 (ka-ra-ka-te-ra).

713702.t: From χαμαί (khamaí, “on the ground”) + λέων (léōn, “lion”); ultimately a calque of Akkadian 𒌨𒈤𒊭𒆠 (nēšu ša qaqqari, “chameleon, reptile”, literally “lion of the ground", "predator that crawls upon the ground”).

713701.t: From a case form of Proto-Indo-European *dʰéǵʰōm (“earth”) (whence also χθών (khthṓn, “earth”)), traditionally taken as a dative.

713768.t: From χάσκω (khắskō, “to yawn; to gape”) + -μα (-mă, result noun suffix).

713722.t: The formation is similar to other bird names, like αἰγυπιός (aigupiós), αἰγωλιός (aigōliós) and ἐρῳδιός (erōidiós). Traditionally derived from χαράδρα (kharádra, “dry bed of a river”), but it could be folk etymology.

713784.t: From χείμερος (kheímeros, “wintry, stormy”) + -ινός (-inós), or directly from Proto-Indo-European [Term?] and cognate with Latin hībernus.

713765.t: Per Rix (LIV), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂-n (“to yawn, to gape”) with inchoative suffix -σκω (-skō).

713799.t: Suppletive comparative of κακός (kakós, “bad”), from an element χερ- (kher-) of disputed origin + comparative suffix *-ϳων (*-jōn).

713783.t: Contraction of χειμάρροος (kheimárrhoos), from χεῖμα (kheîma, “winter”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

713729.t: The formation is similar to κάμαξ (kắmăx, “vine pole; prop”) and πίναξ (pĭ́năx, “board; plank”), and the traditional connection with Lithuanian žer̃ti (“to scrape”) does not explain the Greek formation.

713772.t: Because of its basic meaning "loose, with holes, porous", is quite possible for this adjective to derive from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂-no-s, from *ǵʰeh₂- (“to yawn, hape”), like χάος (kháos, “abyss, chasm”), χαίνω (khaínō), and χάσκω (kháskō, “to gape,…
